name: Carnivorous plants — pitchers, sundews, snap traps
status: 13 archetypal species (full list archived in docs/plant_archive)
notes: Bog and seep plants that live where the soil has no nitrogen and take it from insects instead. Rule they add: they grow ONLY on nutrient-poor ground (peat, sand, wet rock, tepui summits) with high moisture, and their growth reads the local INSECT count instead of soil fertility — a bog full of midges grows fat pitchers; kill the insects and the sundews starve. Their flowers stand far above the traps so the pollinators survive. Sarracenia and Dionaea live in fire-kept pine savanna and bog and need the burns (Phase 9 reads this). Nepenthes are tropical climbers and cliff plants; the great montane ones drown rats and host tree shrews. Bladderworts float in ponds and eat water fleas.

ground.name: Purple pitcher plant

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: tiny green tubular pitchers about 1 cm. Adult an evergreen rosette of fat, curved, jug-like pitchers 10-30 cm lying on the moss, green to deep red with purple veins, with a flared, hairy hood and full of rainwater; it adds only a few pitchers a year.
growth.source: Schnell 2002, Carnivorous Plants of the United States and Canada, and ICPS growing guides (seed needs 4-8 weeks of cold, then germinates in 2-6 weeks; seedlings reach flowering size in about 3-5+ yr; long-lived rhizomes; fire-maintained sunny bogs); Wikipedia S. purpurea (seed falls a median 5 cm from the parent, so plants form clusters)

repro.note: flowers held high on a stalk so pollinators aren't eaten; seed by wind and water

ground.name: Yellow pitcher plant

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: 2 tiny cotyledons, then minute, hairy, green tubular pitchers about 1 cm tall; each year's pitchers are taller, in a fan from a creeping rhizome. Adults have tall (to 90 cm) yellow-green trumpet pitchers with an upright lid and a red throat blotch, flat sword-like leaves (phyllodes) in late summer, and nodding yellow flowers in early spring.
growth.source: Schnell 2002, Carnivorous Plants of the United States and Canada, and ICPS growing guides (seed needs 4-8 weeks of cold, then germinates in 2-6 weeks; seedlings reach flowering size in about 3-5+ yr; long-lived rhizomes; fire-maintained sunny bogs); Flora of N America S. flava (pitchers to 90 cm)

ground.name: Parrot pitcher plant

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: tiny green tubular pitchers. Adult a flat rosette of reclining pitchers 5-20 cm long lying on the ground in a wheel, each ending in a ball-shaped hood like a parrot's beak, speckled with white windows and a small entrance slit; under floodwater they trap tadpoles and small fish.
growth.source: Schnell 2002, Carnivorous Plants of the United States and Canada, and ICPS growing guides (seed needs 4-8 weeks of cold, then germinates in 2-6 weeks; seedlings reach flowering size in about 3-5+ yr; long-lived rhizomes; fire-maintained sunny bogs); Flora of N America S. psittacina (decumbent pitchers 5-30 cm with a globose beaked hood)

ground.name: Giant montane pitcher

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: a tiny rosette of narrow leaves with minute pitchers. For many years it is a slowly widening rosette of broad, leathery leaves with ever bigger, red-purple, urn-shaped lower pitchers resting on the ground, with a broad ribbed rim and a huge vaulted lid; only old plants send out a thick scrambling stem up to several metres.
growth.source: Wikipedia Nepenthes rajah (Kinabalu, 1500-2650 m, open sunny sites; scrambling stem to 6 m, mostly under 3 m; pitchers to 41 x 20 cm; inflorescence to 80-120 cm, flowers any time of year; slow growing); ages estimated from highland Nepenthes cultivation

ground.name: Slender pitcher

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: tiny round cotyledons, then a flat rosette of narrow leaves whose tips grow into miniature pitchers. The rosette bears squat, winged, green to red-speckled 'lower' pitchers resting on the ground; after a year or two a thin, angular stem climbs through scrub, now with slender, wingless, cylindrical 'upper' pitchers on tendrils that coil round supports.
growth.source: Estimated from lowland Nepenthes (Clarke 1997/2001 'Nepenthes of Borneo/Sumatra & Peninsular Malaysia': rosette then climbing stems to several m, dimorphic lower/upper pitchers, weedy species of open disturbed ground); growers' germination data (2-8 weeks)

ground.name: Round-leaved sundew

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds need winter cold, then germinate in spring on wet Sphagnum; the seedling is a tiny flat rosette of round red-haired leaves on long stalks. Each autumn it shrinks to a tight winter bud (hibernaculum) that reopens in April-May; in shade the rosette turns spindly and upright instead of flat.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Drosera rotundifolia (short-lived perennial; flowers every summer once established, Jun-Sep, one flower opening per day; hibernaculum forms in fall and opens Apr-May; very shade intolerant; shallow roots <6 cm); Nordbakken et al. 2004 J. ground.name: Cape sundew

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds germinate readily on wet ground. The seedling is a tiny rosette of short spoon-shaped sticky leaves that grow longer and more strap-like with each new leaf; it reaches flowering size within a year and slowly builds a short stem (4-15 cm) clothed in old dead leaves.
growth.source: Wikipedia Drosera capensis (rosette 10-15 cm, up to 30 cm; short stem 4-15 cm; flowers in summer on 1-2 stalks of 15-30 pale purple flowers; seedlings flower within a year; capsules ripe 4-5 weeks after pollination; self-fertile; wet seeps 0-1800 m; prefers full sun). Lifespan estimated.

ground.name: Forked sundew

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings form a small rosette of simple, unforked, strap- to spoon-shaped sticky leaves; only as the plant matures do leaves become the tall, forked 'Y' blades (and in some forms many-forked fans) on long wiry stalks. Temperate forms die back to a thick rhizome in winter and resprout.
growth.source: Wikipedia Drosera binata (large perennial sundew; leaves up to 60 cm, forked once in the T-form, up to 8 or 30+ points in other forms; SE Australia and NZ below 1000 m; some populations winter-dormant); ICPS guide (seedlings lack forked leaves). Timings and lifespan estimated.

ground.name: Pygmy sundew

growth.juvenile_note: Starts from seed or from gemmae (tiny green brood bodies from the rosette centre in late autumn-winter); within weeks a flat rosette 8-18 mm across of minute round sticky leaves forms, centred on a tuft of silvery stipules. Short-lived: some populations behave as annuals or biennials, and it is easily smothered by taller plants.
growth.source: Wikipedia Drosera pygmaea (rosette 8-18 mm; biennial or annual in parts of its range; small pale flowers on 2.5-7.5 cm stems; open ground, coastal to subalpine in NZ); NZ Plant Conservation Network (gemmae, flowering Oct-Mar); Lowrie, pygmy sundews (short-lived perennial rosettes)

ground.name: Venus flytrap

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two tiny oval cotyledons, then the very first true leaf is already a miniature trap 1-2 mm across. Seedlings form a flat rosette of tiny traps on short leafy stalks, adding larger leaves each year; mature rosettes carry 4-7 traps and later divide underground into small colonies.
growth.source: Wikipedia Venus flytrap (rosette of 4-7 leaves, 3-10 cm; seed germinates without dormancy; 4-5 yr to maturity; lives 20-30 yr in cultivation; full sun, <10% canopy cover, fire every 3-5 yr; winter dormancy); FlytrapCare seed guide (germination 10-30 d)

epiphyte.name: Lowe's pitcher

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: a tiny rosette of narrow leaves tipped with miniature pitchers. For years it stays a slow rosette making rounded, winged lower pitchers; then a stem up to 10 m climbs or hangs from mossy trees and makes the famous upper pitchers: hard, glossy, strongly waisted with a wide flared mouth and a lid bristling with white 'nectar' hairs under which tree shrews feed and leave droppings.
growth.source: Wikipedia Nepenthes lowii (1650-2600 m mossy forest, terrestrial or epiphytic; stem >10 m; gets 57-100% of leaf nitrogen from tree shrew droppings; raceme to 45 cm, capsules ~17 x 4 mm); growth and ages estimated from highland Nepenthes cultivation (very slow)
